entities.name: National University of Córdoba
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The National University of Córdoba (Universidad Nacional de Córdoba, UNC), founded in 1613 by the Jesuits as the Colegio Máximo under Bishop Fernando de Trejo y Sanabria — making it the oldest university in present-day Argentina and the fourth-oldest in Latin America after Santo Domingo (1538), Lima (1551), and Mexico City (1551) — is primarily historically significant as the birthplace of the Latin American University Reform of 1918 (the Córdoba Reform or Grito de Córdoba), which transformed university governance across Latin America and influenced global higher education models.

The 1918 University Reform, launched by student activists at Córdoba in June 1918 with their 'Córdoba Manifesto' (La Juventud Argentina de Córdoba a los Hombres Libres de Sud América), demanded: student co-governance of universities, free public university education, autonomy from state and Church, tenure for professors, and university extension services for working classes. These demands spread across Latin America with extraordinary speed — within a decade, most major Latin American countries had adopted variations of the Córdoba model, fundamentally reshaping higher education governance across the region.

The Córdoba Reform's influence extended globally: its model of student participation in university governance was adopted in varying degrees across Latin America and influenced university reform movements in Asia, Africa, and Europe. The university today has approximately 130,000 students across faculties in law, medicine, engineering, natural sciences, and philosophy — making it Argentina's largest university and maintaining its historical role as a center of Argentine intellectual and political life.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The National University of Córdoba — the oldest Argentine university (1613), birthplace of the 1918 Latin American University Reform that transformed higher education governance across an entire continent, and home to the student movement that gave working classes access to free university education — is one of the Western Hemisphere's most historically consequential universities.
